title: How an independent school should write an about page
metaTitle: How an independent school writes about
excerpt: Name the adults a child will meet and the part of the day they own. Skip the founding myth unless it changes the decision to visit.

faqs.question: Who belongs on a school about page?
faqs.answer: The head if they are actually in the week, the pattern of class teachers, the person at the gate, and the person who answers a visit request. Give names, roles, and the slice of the day each one owns. Update the page when a named person leaves.

faqs.question: When is a founding story useful?
faqs.answer: When it explains a constraint a child will meet, such as a house with the youngest classes on the ground floor. A coat of arms and a list of notable alumni can follow the names, or they can stay in a speech. Open with the adults.

faqs.question: What should the page ask a parent to do next?
faqs.answer: Visit, or inquire with the child's year. Repeat the limit that most often changes the choice, such as the end of the day or the ages you do not teach. Keep the long form on the contact path so this page stays about people.

markdown:
An independent school about page should prove that specific adults stand behind the day. Name who teaches and who runs the gate, and say why a parent deciding on years of a child's life should care. Skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision to visit or inquire.

Google's helpful-content guidance treats "who" as a trust question. A visitor should be able to tell who is responsible, and the page should show experience that comes from doing the work. An about page is that answer for a school. A crest, a Latin motto, or a tale about a founder in the nineteenth century does not substitute for a name, a role, and the part of the day that person owns.

## Who is in the building

Start with the adults a parent and a child will actually meet. The head, if the head is present in the week and not only in the portrait. The class teacher pattern: whether a child has one main adult. The person at the gate at pickup. The registrar who answers the visit request. Give each a name, a role, and the slice of the day they are accountable for.

A portrait helps when it is the person, in the school, dressed as they dress for work. A portrait hurts when it is a hallway with a shield and no face. Parents are deciding whether to hand you a child. Faces are part of that decision. If someone prefers not to be pictured, use the name and the role. Absence of a photograph is honest. A stock smile beside the crest is not.

Say what each person decides. "Ms Adeyemi teaches year 5 and is the adult who speaks to you if the day goes wrong for that class." That sentence does more than a paragraph about her love of learning. Authority in a school is operational. Who phones home. Who cannot promise a learning-support plan the school does not staff. Who stands outside at 3:20 even in the rain.

If the staff is small, say it is small. Small is often why a parent is looking at you. They need to know the smallness is real and stable, not a costume of "close-knit community" with no names. "Close-knit" without names is a genre. Names are the proof.

## Why this parent cares

The reader is not your historian. They are choosing a childhood's weekdays. They care about the about page only where it changes a risk they can feel. Will someone notice if my child goes quiet? Who do I write to? Is the head a person on the corridor or a signature on a prospectus? Will the promise in the inquiry be the promise on the first day?

Write toward those worries. "Each class has a teacher who stays with them through the year, and you can reach that teacher through the office." That is a reason to care. "Our story began with a vision" does not touch the worry. It asks for patience the parent is spending on the other two schools.

You can still be warm. Warmth is a pattern: a head who knows the children's names by October, a gate that is staffed, a refusal to admit a child whose needs you cannot meet rather than a hopeful yes. Character, on this page, is a pattern of decisions. It is not a list of adjectives approved by a committee.

If you have a point of view that changes the visit, put it high. A faith practice that is part of the day. No selection by test. A uniform. Phones kept in bags. The about page is a fair place for the point of view, as long as the visit is still one click away. A point of view that is only atmospheric, "we believe in wonder," needs a concrete partner or it will not survive the comparison.

## When a founding story earns its place

A founding story earns its place when it explains a constraint the child will meet. The school occupies a converted house, so the youngest classes are on the ground floor and the stair is part of the older children's day. The school was started for a particular neighborhood, so the admissions preference is the one you print, not a vibe. The hall fits the whole school only if the youngest sit on the floor, which is why assembly looks the way it looks.

That kind of origin changes the decision to visit. It tells the parent what they are walking into and why you did not become a different institution. It is useful.

An origin that does not earn its place is the voyage of prestige. A coat of arms. A sentence about educating the leaders of tomorrow. A long walk through distinguished alumni who are not the point of a Tuesday in year 3. These can be true and still be irrelevant to the decision in front of a family. If you want them, put them after the names and the hours, in a short passage. Do not open with them. The first screen is still a decision screen.

Read the origin aloud and ask: would this sentence change whether we visit, or which age we ask about? If the answer is no, the sentence can live in a speech. It does not need the top of the page.

## What to cut from the institutional essay

Cut the adjectives you would be embarrassed to say to a parent at the gate. Passionate. World-class. Nurturing excellence. Nestled. Cut "not like other schools" unless the next sentence is the specific difference: one teacher all year, a day that ends at 3:20, no entrance test.

Cut honors and badges unless you can say what they were for, in a few words a parent understands. A row of accreditation marks is not an about page. Sometimes one sentence is enough. Sometimes silence is more accurate than a logo you cannot explain when asked.

Cut the group photograph where nobody is identified. Cut the timeline that reads like a commemorative booklet. Keep one fact if it explains the day a child will have: a new library that is actually one room with a roster, a science bench added in the senior years, a playground that is small and supervised.

Cut a letter from the head that never mentions the parent's decision. If you keep a letter, make it short enough to finish, sign it with the name people meet, and end on how to visit or inquire. A letter that ends on "we look forward to welcoming your family" has not said how a family becomes welcome.

The essay is finished when a skeptical person could tell who is responsible for their child on a Thursday. If the draft cannot pass that test without the adjectives, it is still a costume.

## Names, roles, and the gate

Put names where they can be checked against the visit. The person who hosts the open morning should be a person the page has named, or the page should say the host varies and the role does not. Alignment is a small operational task and a large trust task. Parents talk to each other after tours. The site should match what they saw.

Roles should be current. Update the page when a teacher leaves, in the same week if they were named, not at the next redesign. An about page with a former class teacher is worse than a short page, because a child may ask for an adult who cannot appear. Keep the roster short enough that you will maintain it. You do not need every colleague on day one. You need the pattern and the people a new family will rely on.

If the head is new, say so, and say who is steady. Pretending continuity you do not have is a fast way to lose a family that values steadiness. "The head joined in September. The year-group teachers are unchanged" is a clear structure. Families can decide what they think of it. They cannot decide what you hid.

The gate itself can be described as a place: which door, what time, who wears the high-visibility coat if that is how you are found. Independent schools often fail this in person because the entrance is modest. The about page can prevent a parent and a nervous child from circling the block. That is a kindness and a proof that you have watched a first morning.

## Hand the page back to the visit

The about page is not the last step. A parent who trusts the adults still needs a day they can see, and a place in a year that exists. Close with visit or inquire, in a sentence. "If the way we staff the day fits, book a visit for your child's year." Repeat the constraint that most often changes the decision, in one line, so they carry it with them: the end time, the stair, the ages you do not teach.

Do not add an inquiry form longer than the biographies. The contact path can hold the form. This page's action remains the visit. A form here teaches that joining the school is a correspondence, when the next honest step is usually to walk the corridor while it is full.

If you mention a limit, keep it consistent with the admissions and the day pages. The about page is where people go to resolve doubt. A contradiction between "a calm, small community" here and a class size you never state reopens the doubt. One description. Use it everywhere.

Invite a teacher to delete one line from their own paragraph. The line they delete is usually the one written to make them sound grand. Grand is not the goal. Recognizable on a Thursday is the goal.

## Where proof goes next

Names establish who. They do not yet show a hard decision about the day itself: a constraint, a choice, and the students in the middle of it. That belongs on a proof page. [How to show one true decision about the school day](/blog/proof-pages-for-an-independent-school) is the next piece, because a pleasant biography can still leave a parent unsure what their child will do between nine and three.

When you want help choosing which sentences earn the page, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the current about text and this term's staff list. The gap between those two documents is the rewrite.
